name: Jade Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Jade. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, and your name won't be attached to anything. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yes, that's fine. I'll warn you, I have opinions about this, so you might get more than you asked for. I've been freelancing for about three years, since I finished my languages degree.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Opinions are welcome. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Two days a week I'm at the city hospital or the legal aid clinic, interpreting Spanish and English for patients and clients. I'll sit with a mum on the children's ward while the doctor explains a feeding tube, or with a man going through an eviction notice. The other days I'm at my kitchen table translating documents for a non-profit language service and two agencies: school letters, tenancy papers, discharge notes. I love the hospital days, but they wear me out, and I'm still slow on the written work.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out most, and what do you like most?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: What wears me out is the written work, honestly, because my agency editor sends back a lot of red pen. Last month I translated 'deposit' three different ways in one eight-page tenancy agreement. What I like is the moment in a hospital room when a scared mum finally understands what's happening to her child. Nobody's paying me for that feeling, but it's why I do this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds like now, which isn't as comfortable as people think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, and I'd say it loudly in my union branch chat. Translation needs a person who understands the human in front of them, and a stalled AI would prove it. I'd probably post something a bit smug, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, even a small change touches me. The agencies already offer 'post-editing', which means fixing a machine's draft for less than half the normal rate. One of my agencies cut my document work by about a fifth this year, so a plateau still squeezes the written side I'm still learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep turning down post-editing jobs, the way I do now. I'd ask the hospital for a third interpreting day each week, because nobody is trying to cheapen that part yet. And I'd finally sit the community interpreting certificate next spring, which costs about 900, and I can afford it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, but not scared. Sam, my partner, teaches at the secondary school, and we have about nine months of savings plus the money my grandmother left me. It's a low hum, not an alarm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you turn down post-editing jobs. What does that cost you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe 300 a month, roughly, and my editor has hinted the agency will stop calling if I keep saying no. I can afford to turn down the cheap machine-fixing work, which is a privilege lots of translators in my union branch don't have. I try not to forget that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about, if this is how it goes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older people who only do written work from home. There's a woman in my branch, Pilar, who has done court documents for twenty years, and her rates have dropped every year since the machines got decent. Even in a plateau, she's the one carrying the cut, not the tech firms.

say: Translation still needs a **person** who understands the human in the room.
A **stalled AI** would prove my union branch was right all along.
think: Agencies already push **post-editing** at less than half my normal rate.
One agency cut my **document work** by about a fifth this year.
Even a plateau keeps squeezing the **written side** I'm still learning.
do: **Turn down** post-editing jobs, at a cost of roughly 300 a month.
Ask the hospital for a **third interpreting day** each week.
Sit the community interpreting **certificate** next spring for about 900.
feel: **Uneasy**, but more a low hum than an alarm.
Steadied by **savings**, an inheritance and her partner's teaching pay.
S0.quote: I can afford to turn down the cheap machine-fixing work, which is a privilege lots of translators in my union branch don't have.
fieldNote: Her **principled refusal** of post-editing is paid for by savings and an inheritance.
She treats **interpreting days** as the safe half of her work.
Her worry points **outward**, at older colleagues like Pilar, before herself.

steps.text: Keep refusing post-editing jobs from the two agencies
Ask the city hospital for a third interpreting day
Sit the community interpreting certificate next spring

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Oh, that one's much closer to what I'm scared of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say: hospitals and courts must keep human interpreters by law. I'd be at every union branch meeting, and I'd share every story about a machine getting a dosage wrong. Publicly I'd sound angry more than worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my written work is gone in that picture. Documents are exactly the 'writing and checking' on that card, and I'm junior and slow, so I'm first out. The agencies won't need me, and I'll be left with interpreting, which is maybe half my income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start this month by moving my hours toward the hospital and the legal aid clinic, and dropping the agencies before they drop me. I'd sit the interpreting certificate and then start on the court interpreting exam, which takes about a year. I'd also help the branch push our city council to require human interpreters in health and housing appointments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor is tilting. I know I won't go hungry, and that makes me feel a bit guilty. But I picked this job because I love languages, and watching half of it vanish before I'm even good at it feels like a door shutting in my face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Sam that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him we can live on his salary and my savings for a while, but I don't want to. Sam (my partner) would say 'just use the tools like everyone else', and we'd have the same argument we always have. I'd go to bed angry and wake up and study for the court exam.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd drop the agencies before they drop you. Isn't that a big risk for someone still learning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and I've thought about it. The agencies are where I get the editing that makes me better, so leaving them slows me down. But I'd rather learn in a hospital room than learn to be a machine's proofreader at half the pay.

say: Hospitals and courts must keep **human interpreters** by law.
I'd share every story of a **machine mistake** in a patient's care.
think: My **written work** is exactly the writing and checking on that card.
Being **junior and slow** puts me first out at the agencies.
Interpreting is maybe **half my income**, and that's what would be left.
do: **Shift hours** to the hospital and legal aid clinic this month.
Take the **court interpreting exam** after the certificate, about a year's work.
Push the **city council**, with the branch, to require human interpreters.
feel: **Angry and guilty** at once, because she knows she won't go hungry.
Like a **door shutting** before she has even got good at the job.
S1.quote: I'd rather learn in a hospital room than learn to be a machine's proofreader at half the pay.
fieldNote: She expects to **lose half** her income and says so plainly.
Her **refusal of AI** is now a career choice, not just a principle.
She knowingly gives up the **editing feedback** she needs to improve.

steps.text: Drop agency document work and move hours to hospital interpreting
Study for the court interpreting exam over the next year
Lobby the city council with the union branch for human interpreters

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's before I'd even finish the court exam.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a choice made by a handful of tech companies, and governments are letting it happen. I'd march, I'd sign everything, and I'd tell anyone who'd listen that people in hospitals deserve a human voice. Online I'd be furious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, if AI can do any thinking work by 2028, interpreting is thinking work, even if I'm sitting in the room. Hospitals will buy a tablet that does it in forty languages for less than my day rate. I'd have the language skills and nothing to sell them to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right away I'd stop spending on the certificate and keep the savings whole, because nine months of money matters more than a credential nobody wants. I'd lean on the union branch to demand a public fund for retraining people like me. And since robots come about three years later, I'd look seriously at hands-on care work, maybe as a healthcare assistant on the same wards I interpret on now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, mostly. I picture the mum on the children's ward talking to a tablet, and I hate it more than I fear for myself. Then I think about myself, and I'm frightened too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said hands-on care work. What would that mean in practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the ward manager I know, Grace, about the healthcare assistant training they run in-house. Grace (the ward manager) has told me before that I'm good with families, so maybe that counts for something. It's lower pay than I get now, maybe a third less, but it's three more years of being needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years before robots actually buy you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to save and time to get out of the line of fire. If thinking work goes in 2028 and hands-on work goes in 2031, then I'd be moving into the slower lane, not a safe one. I'm not stupid about that, but slower is still something.

say: A handful of **tech companies** chose this, and governments let it happen.
People in hospitals deserve a **human voice**, not a tablet.
think: Interpreting is **thinking work**, so it goes in 2028 like the rest.
Hospitals would buy a **tablet** for less than my day rate.
do: **Stop spending** on the certificate and keep nine months of savings whole.
Press the union branch for a **public retraining fund**.
Ask about **healthcare assistant** training on the wards she knows.
feel: **Sick** at the thought of a scared mum talking to a tablet.
**Frightened** for herself once the anger fades.
S2.quote: If thinking work goes in 2028 and hands-on work goes in 2031, then I'd be moving into the slower lane, not a safe one.
fieldNote: She sees clearly that **interpreting** counts as thinking work too.
The **three-year gap** before robots shapes her move toward care work.
Accepts about **a third less pay** to stay useful on the wards.

steps.text: Stop paying for the certificate and keep savings untouched
Push the union branch for a public retraining fund
Ask the ward manager about healthcare assistant training

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a bit more breathing room, but not much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly I'd say the same as before, louder: we need laws now, while there's still time. I'd be the person at the branch meeting with the petition. I'd also say it to Sam's colleagues at dinner, which he'd hate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is long enough to get properly good at interpreting and then lose it anyway. That's the cruel part. I'd be at my best in 2030 and out of work in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still take the certificate this year, because five years of better-paid interpreting is real money to save. I'd put a fixed 500 a month into savings from now on. And I'd help the union branch write to our member of parliament about keeping human interpreters in courts and hospitals, before the date arrives, not after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy in my stomach all the time, I think. There'd be a calendar in my head counting down. But I'd feel less helpless than with two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first thing you'd cut, if you're saving 500 a month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The weekend trips to see my sister in the next city, and eating out. Sam and I eat out twice a week, which is silly. Cutting that alone is most of the 500.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be at your best and then lose it. Does that change whether you'd study at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've gone back and forth. Part of me says why bother. But I'd rather be good at something for five years than half good at it, and the money from being good is what buys me the next door.

say: We need **laws now**, while there's still time to act.
Courts and hospitals must keep **human interpreters** past 2031.
think: Five years is enough to **get good** and still lose it.
I'd peak around **2030** and be out of work by 2031.
do: Take the interpreting **certificate** this year for better-paid days.
Save a fixed **500 a month** from now on.
Write to the **member of parliament** with the union branch.
feel: A **countdown** running in her head every day.
**Less helpless** than with two years' warning.
S3.quote: Five years is long enough to get properly good at interpreting and then lose it anyway.
fieldNote: The **cruel timing** of peaking just before the cut bothers her most.
Extra time turns into **saving**, not a career change yet.
Her politics move from anger to **lobbying** with a deadline.

steps.text: Take the community interpreting certificate this year
Save 500 a month by cutting weekend trips and eating out
Write to the local member of parliament with the union branch

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Okay. I'd be thirty-seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have a decade to build something fair: retraining paid for by the companies that profit, and protected human roles in health and justice. I'd want the union to treat it as a ten-year campaign, not a panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years feels survivable. I could have a real career in interpreting, save a lot, and still change direction in my early thirties. It's not a happy picture, but it's one I can plan in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the certificate and the court exam, and take the court work, which pays better. I'd keep saving, maybe 400 a month. Around year five I'd start a part-time nursing degree, because by then I'd know which way it's going, and nursing has years of hands-on work left after the thinking work goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, but sad underneath. I'd still be counting, just with a longer calendar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why nursing, rather than something else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I already spend my days on wards and I like it there. Sam (my partner) says I'd make a better nurse than half the ones he knows, which isn't fair to nurses, but it's nice of him. And robots come later than the AI, so it buys me years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you'd never use AI tools. In ten years, does that hold?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes. I'd rather leave translation with clean hands than spend ten years training the thing that replaces my friends. That's stubborn, I know.

say: We have a decade to build a **fair transition**, paid by the companies.
The union should run a **ten-year campaign**, not a panic.
think: Ten years feels **survivable**, with a real interpreting career first.
I could still **change direction** in my early thirties.
do: Finish the certificate and the **court exam**, then take court work.
Start a part-time **nursing degree** around year five.
feel: Still counting, just on a **longer calendar**.
S4.quote: I'd rather leave translation with clean hands than spend ten years training the thing that replaces my friends.
fieldNote: The **decade** turns fear into a two-stage plan: interpreting, then nursing.
Her **refusal of AI** holds even with ten years to adapt.
She still expects to **lose the job**, so worry stays real.

steps.text: Pass the court interpreting exam and take court work
Save about 400 a month for the move
Start a part-time nursing degree around year five
Push the union for a ten-year transition campaign

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, without a doubt, because there's no time to get good at anything new. What would help is a law that keeps human interpreters in hospitals and courts, and paid retraining that doesn't come out of my own savings. My savings are meant for a flat, not for fixing what tech companies broke.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the patients. Everyone talks about translators losing work, but a scared mum on a ward is the one who loses most. A tablet won't notice that a scared mum has stopped listening because she's crying.

headlineQuote: A tablet won't notice that a scared mum has stopped listening because she's crying.
portrait: Jade is a 27-year-old **Spanish-English** freelancer who interprets in a hospital and translates documents at home.
She refuses **AI tools** on principle and turns down cheaper post-editing work.
Savings, an inheritance and her partner's **teaching pay** let her afford those principles.
Across the scenarios she moves toward **interpreting**, then healthcare work, and campaigns through her union.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there'd be no time to get good at anything new.
whatWouldHelp: A law keeping **human interpreters** in hospitals and courts.
Paid **retraining** that doesn't come out of her own savings.
